:step/content.:tutorial/content:
The derivative of the natural logarithm is the reciprocal function:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( \ln x \right)= \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

We'll prove this result in a future lesson.

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
The derivative of the natural logarithm is the reciprocal function:

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( \ln x \right)= \dfrac{1}{x}
$$

We apply our formula and get

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}   & = \left(5\ln x\right)'\  
                                                    & = 5 (\ln x)'\
                                                    &=5\cdot \dfrac{1}{x}\
                                                    &= \dfrac{5}{x}.
						  

}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating the Product of a Constant and the Natural Logarithm Function

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\eqalign{
			f'(x) &= \left(2\ln x+x^2-1\right)'\
			&=2 \cdot \dfrac{1}{x}+2x-0\
			&=\dfrac{2}{x}+2x.

}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating a Sum Containing a Natural Logarithm Function

:step/content.:tutorial/content:
For a general logarithm of base $a,$ the derivative is given by

$$
\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{ \textrm{d} x}\left( \log_a x \right)= \dfrac{1}{x\ln a}.
$$

Also, recall that whenever $\log$ is written without a base, we can assume that it represents the base $10.$ So, we have

$$
\log x =  \log_{10} x.
$$

Therefore,

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{d}{dx}(\operatorname{log}x) & =\frac{d}{dx}({log}_{10}x)=\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}10}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Note:** To see where this rule comes from, we can use the change-of-base formula as shown below.

$$
\log_a x = \dfrac{\ln x}{\ln a}
$$

Taking the derivative and using the fact that $\ln a$ is a constant, then, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}({log}_{a}x) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\frac{\operatorname{ln}x}{\operatorname{ln}a}) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}a}\cdot \frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}x}(\operatorname{ln}x) \\  & =\frac{1}{\operatorname{ln}a}\cdot \frac{1}{x} \\  & =\frac{1}{x\operatorname{ln}a}.\end{aligned}
$$
:step/content.:tutorial/title: Differentiating a Logarithmic Function with a General Base

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
Here, we apply our formula for the derivative when the base of the logarithm is a number other than $e.$ By doing so, we obtain

$$
\eqalign{
			\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}&=\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(4\log_3 x\right)\
									 &=4\dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left(\log_3 x\right)\
									 &=4\cdot\dfrac{1}{x \ln 3}\
									&=\dfrac{4}{x \ln 3}.

}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Differentiating a Logarithmic Function With a General Base

:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/problem: Given that $y= \log_4 x + \ln x$,  find the slope of the tangent at $x=1.$
:knowledge-point/canonical-example.:question/worked-solution:
To find the slope of the tangent at a given point, we have to find $\dfrac {\textrm{d}y} {\textrm{d}x}$ at that point.

Taking the derivative, we have

$$
\eqalign{
\dfrac{\textrm{d}y}{\textrm{d}x}
		&= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}\left( \log_4 x + \ln x \right)\
		&= \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\log_4 x) + \dfrac{\textrm{d}}{\textrm{d}x}(\ln x )\
		&= \dfrac{1}{x\ln 4} + \dfrac{1}{x}.
}
$$

Therefore, the slope of the tangent at $x=1$ is

$$
\begin{aligned}{\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}x}|}_{x=1} & ={(\frac{1}{xln⁡4}+\frac{1}{x})|}_{x=1} \\  & =\frac{1}{ln⁡4}+1.\end{aligned}
$$

:step/content.:knowledge-point/title: Calculating the Slope of the Tangent Line of a Logarithmic Function at a Point
